historical_timeline.summary: Meets Sri Ramakrishna; takes monastic vows in 1887.
Speaks at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago; teaches in the West until 1897.
Writes that he has diabetes; goes to Darjeeling on his physicians' advice.
Founds the Ramakrishna Mission Association; writes of lifelong trouble falling asleep.
Leaves for Darjeeling; plague relief in Calcutta; travels north from May 11.
Returns to Belur pallid and ill, with suffocating attacks of asthma.
Writes that the diabetes has gone and asthma has come in its place.
Second visit to the West, returning to the Belur Math in December 1900.
Writes of albuminuria for three years and a bleed in the right eye; asthma, diabetes and dropsy in his last illness.
Dies at the Belur Math at 39.

claims.statement: In March and April 1897, soon after his return to India, he wrote that he had diabetes. On 16 March he wrote: "The work has broken me down completely, and I have got 'diabetes', an incurable disease"; on 26 March: "The result of this steady work in the West and the tremendous work of a month in India upon the Bengalee constitution is 'diabetes'. It is a hereditary foe," adding that "Eating only meat and drinking no water seems to be the only way to prolong life"; and on 7 April that he had been "attacked by 'Diabetes', a fell disease" and had gone to Darjeeling, cool and "very good for the disease," where the doctors did not want him to move about. A biography says he went to Darjeeling on the advice of physicians.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diabetes, at about 34, to which the modern diagnosis is linked. He called it hereditary; no relative is named. How the diagnosis was made is not recorded (urine sugar is likely but not stated).

claims.statement: On 29 May 1897, from Almora, he wrote to a physician disciple that he was taking the medicines sent to him, riding morning and evening and feeling very strong, but that "I never in my life could sleep as soon as I got into bed. I must toss for at least two hours," that he felt hot after the evening meal, that "There has not been any thirst even though the days are fearfully hot," and that he was afraid of "getting fat on a too much milk diet."

His feet swelled ... He could hardly close his eyes in sleep," and on a physician's strict regimen he avoided water and salt, for twenty-one days taking no water at all.

claims.statement: He died at the Belur Math on the night of 4 July 1902, at 39, after an hour of meditation; a brother monk recalled "a little blood in his nostrils, about his mouth, and in his eyes." The physicians gave the cause as "apoplexy or sudden failure of the heart"; the monks held that he had left his body in samadhi.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, stated without detail and with respect for the monks' understanding of his death.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Diagnose and classify diabetes in a 35-year-old South Asian man at a near-normal BMI (ADA screens Asian Americans from a BMI of 23 because South Asians develop type 2 diabetes at lower weights and younger ages): confirm with A1c and fasting glucose, test GAD antibodies and C-peptide to exclude type 1 and slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes, and record the decision. Then treat by shared decision with metformin and, once moderately increased albuminuria is confirmed, an SGLT2 inhibitor; build a mostly vegetarian, culturally fitting nutrition plan with a dietitian around his monastic diet; plan safe religious fasting with medication adjustment (IDF-DAR guidance, adapted from Ramadan to Hindu fasts); screen and protect the kidneys (UACR, eGFR, blood pressure with an ARB), eyes and lipids; treat long-standing insomnia without hypnotics; and diagnose and treat adult-onset asthma on GINA track 1, managing the steroid-induced hyperglycemia of an exacerbation. His diet, fasting and monastic practice are his to decide; the clinic adapts to them.

Monogenic diabetes is unlikely without a clear three-generation pattern. In South Asians type 2 diabetes appears earlier and at lower BMI, with more insulin resistance for a given weight, which is why ADA screens Asian Americans from a BMI of 23. Question 2: insulin is not needed now. He has no ketosis, his own insulin secretion is good and the A1c is below 10 percent; his weight loss reflects glucose spilling into the urine and should stop with treatment
Question 5: 46 mg/g on one sample, which hyperglycemia can raise; it needs two of three abnormal samples over three to six months before diabetic kidney disease is diagnosed

recommendations: Question 3: start metformin extended-release with the evening meal, 500 mg for a week, then 1000 mg, rising to 2000 mg if tolerated; extended-release taken with the meal that ends a fast suits his fasts. A second tablet now would also be reasonable at this A1c, but starting with metformin and diet and reviewing in about five weeks is safe and is his preference. Avoid sulfonylureas, which cause hypoglycemia during fasts. A GLP-1 receptor agonist is not the first choice for a man who has just lost weight unintentionally and prefers tablets
